claims.text: High configurational entropy suppresses large-scale elemental segregation in multi-principal-element nanoalloys at high temperatures.
High configurational entropy suppresses grain coarsening in multi-principal-element nanoalloys at high temperatures.
Suppression of segregation and grain coarsening gives high-entropy nanoalloys greater structural and chemical stability than lower-entropy alloys.
The proposed initial material is a nominally homogeneous nanoscale alloy containing five principal components.
Local chemical disorder constrains long-range diffusion.
Elevated configurational entropy lowers the free-energy driving force for phase separation.
The entropy-related reduction in the driving force for phase separation slows grain growth during high-temperature exposure.
The entropy-related reduction in the driving force for phase separation inhibits elemental segregation during high-temperature exposure.
After identical thermal exposure, the high-entropy nanoalloy will retain finer grains than the lower-entropy baseline.
After identical thermal exposure, the high-entropy nanoalloy will exhibit less elemental segregation than the lower-entropy baseline.
After identical thermal exposure, the high-entropy nanoalloy will form fewer secondary phases than the lower-entropy baseline.
Conventional low-entropy alloys with fewer principal elements typically undergo more pronounced grain growth at the same temperatures.
Conventional low-entropy alloys with fewer principal elements typically undergo more pronounced segregation at the same temperatures.
The proposed stabilizing effects are most pronounced below the melting temperatures of the constituent elements.
At sufficiently high temperatures, phase segregation can occur despite high configurational entropy.
At sufficiently long annealing times, phase segregation can occur despite high configurational entropy.
The exact alloy composition may affect high-temperature stability.
